questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. AI audit universe
questions.question: An IS audit manager builds next year's AI audit universe solely from the model registry that the data science team's training platform fills automatically. What is the GREATEST concern with this approach?

options.A: The registry omits AI features embedded in purchased software and services
options.B: The registry still lists retired models that no longer decide anything
options.C: The registry does not name a business owner for each model
options.D: The registry does not record each model's programming framework

questions.key_concept: A risk-based AI audit universe starts from a complete inventory, including AI embedded in purchased products, before any ranking.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the list came from and which kinds of AI that source could never contain.
questions.correct_explanation: An audit universe must be complete before it can be ranked. A registry the training platform fills lists only models trained there, so AI embedded in purchased software, cloud services and business-unit tools, often the highest-impact uses, never reaches the plan. A missing model owner is a real governance gap, but the audit can test and report it once the model is listed; an AI use never listed is never audited.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because stale entries clutter a universe. But retired models are easy to rank low; AI uses that never appear cannot be ranked at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because every model needs a named owner. But a missing owner is a gap the audit can find and report; AI the registry never lists is never audited.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting for a technically minded auditor. But the programming framework does not set audit priority; the likelihood and impact of harm to people and the business do.

tips: Eliminate: D adds technical detail that does not set audit priority, and B flags retired entries that a risk ranking simply rates low.
Final two: A beats C because a missing owner is a gap the audit can test once a model is listed, but AI the registry never lists never reaches the plan.
Exam cue: completeness of the AI audit universe comes before ranking it. Look for embedded, purchased and shadow AI that a builders' list misses.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Sampling for fairness
questions.question: A telecom's phone-financing model excludes age from its inputs. Applicants over 70 are 3% of its decisions. An IS auditor plans a random sample of 60 decisions. Which change BEST supports testing for age bias?

options.A: Draw the sample from the model's training data instead
options.B: Stratify by age band and oversample the oldest band
options.C: Double the random sample to 120 decisions across age groups
options.D: Select the decisions the model scored with highest confidence

questions.key_concept: Fairness testing needs samples stratified by the groups at risk, sized so each group has enough decisions to compare.
questions.pre_read: Work out how many cases from the small group each sample would actually contain.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaving age out of the inputs does not prevent age bias, because other inputs can act as proxies, so outcomes are tested by age. A random sample of 60 would hold about two applicants aged over 70, too few to compare approval rates. Stratifying by age band and oversampling the oldest band fixes that; doubling the random sample still yields only about four older applicants.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because bias often starts in training data. But the objective concerns live decisions, and training records do not show how real applicants were treated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because larger samples give more confidence. But doubling a random sample still yields only a handful of older applicants, too few to compare outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confident scores look like clear cases. But the most confident decisions are the least likely to show errors, and the choice skews the sample further.

tips: Eliminate: A tests training data when the risk sits in live decisions, and D picks the cases least likely to reveal model errors.
Final two: B beats C because a larger random sample still holds only a handful of older applicants; oversampling the oldest band guarantees enough of them to compare.
Exam cue: test AI outcomes by group even when the model never uses the group attribute. A small group needs its own stratum, or the sample cannot see it.

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test, standards audit, concept review).

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing human review
questions.question: A delivery platform's model recommends deactivating couriers. Policy requires a supervisor to review each one, and approval is a single checkbox. Which test gives the IS auditor the BEST evidence that the review operates effectively?

options.A: Inspect the review procedure and each supervisor's training record
options.B: Confirm every logged deactivation carries a supervisor's approval
options.C: Rerun sampled recommendations through the current production model
options.D: Analyze override rates and review times across all deactivations

questions.key_concept: Human oversight of AI is tested by reviewer behavior, such as override rates and review time, not by sign-offs alone.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each test would prove about how the control worked during the period.
questions.correct_explanation: A checked box cannot show that anyone judged the case. Override rates and time spent per review show whether supervisors engage with recommendations or defer to the model, the pattern called automation bias. Confirming that every deactivation carries an approval, option B, is the runner-up: it proves the step happened, not that oversight works.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because procedures and training support a control. But they show design and readiness, not how supervisors actually review over the period.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because full coverage is a classic operating test. But a checkbox on every case proves the step happened, not that supervisors judged anything.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it tests the model, not the supervisors, and today's model may differ from the one that decided.

tips: Eliminate: A inspects design documents rather than operation, and C tests the model instead of the human review.
Final two: D beats B because a sign-off proves the step happened; override rates and review times show whether supervisors actually judge each case.
Exam cue: test human oversight of AI by what reviewers do, such as overrides and time per case, not by the presence of approvals.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Reperformance
questions.question: A marketplace's seller-risk model places holds on payouts and is retrained monthly. An IS auditor wants to confirm that sampled payout holds were produced as logged. Which procedure gives the auditor the MOST reliable evidence?

options.A: Rerun the sampled inputs through the current production model version
options.B: Inspect the model card's description of the input features
options.C: Rerun the sampled inputs through the model version that decided them
options.D: Ask the data scientists how each sampled decision was reached

questions.key_concept: Reperforming an AI decision needs the same model version and logged inputs; retraining makes today's version a different model.
questions.pre_read: Notice how often the model changes, and what that means for rerunning old decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Reperformance is strong evidence when it recreates the conditions of the original decision. Because the model is retrained monthly, only the version that made each decision, given the same logged inputs, should reproduce it. Running the inputs through today's model tests a different model, so mismatches could reflect retraining rather than error, and matches prove nothing about the past decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the current model is easy to run. But monthly retraining makes it a different model, so its outputs cannot confirm past decisions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model cards describe inputs. But a description of features cannot show that any sampled decision was produced as logged.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data scientists know the model. But their explanation is inquiry, the weakest evidence, and cannot show what the model actually output.

tips: Eliminate: D relies on inquiry of the model's builders, and B inspects documentation that describes the model but cannot prove any decision.
Final two: C beats A because monthly retraining changes the model; only the version that made the decision can reproduce it.
Exam cue: to reperform an AI decision, match the model version and inputs used at the time. Versioning is what makes reperformance possible.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Rating findings
questions.question: An IS auditor is rating four AI findings for the audit committee. Which finding should the auditor rate as the GREATEST concern?

options.A: A coding assistant's prompts are not logged for later review
options.B: A forecasting model drifted, raising warehouse stock costs by 2%
options.C: A model suspending mobile-money accounts offers no appeal route
options.D: A new marketing text generator lacks a completed model card

questions.key_concept: AI findings are rated by likelihood and impact on people and the business; high-impact decisions with no appeal route rate highest.
questions.pre_read: For each finding, ask who is harmed, how badly, and whether a wrong decision can be corrected.
questions.correct_explanation: Rating weighs likelihood and impact, counting harm to people as well as to the business. Suspending a mobile-money account can cut someone off from wages and payments, and with no appeal route, wrong suspensions cannot be corrected. The forecasting drift has a measurable cost, but it is a modest financial effect that management can absorb and correct, with no direct harm to individuals.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because missing logs weaken accountability. But an internal coding tool's prompts carry far lower impact than unappealable decisions about customers' money.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it has a measured business cost. But a modest, correctable cost increase weighs less than unappealable decisions that cut people off from their money.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because model cards are expected documentation. But a missing card on a low-impact marketing tool is a documentation gap, not direct harm.

tips: Eliminate: A is a logging gap on a low-impact internal coding tool, and D is a documentation gap on a low-impact marketing tool; neither harms people directly.
Final two: C beats B because unappealable decisions that cut people off from their money outweigh a modest, correctable cost increase.
Exam cue: rate AI findings by likelihood and impact, counting harm to people as well as to the business. High-impact decisions about individuals with no recourse rate highest.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. AI-drafted findings
questions.question: An audit manager sees that a generative AI tool drafted an IS auditor's findings from the work papers and gave each a cause the papers never mention. What should the manager require FIRST?

options.A: Disclose in the report that an AI tool drafted the findings
options.B: Have the auditor check each statement against the evidence
options.C: Ask management to confirm the causes that the tool added
options.D: Have the tool redraft the findings strictly from the work papers

questions.key_concept: The auditor stays accountable for conclusions an AI tool helped draft and verifies each against the evidence before issue.
questions.pre_read: Ask who signs the report and what makes each finding supportable.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative tools fill gaps with plausible content, and causes the work papers never mention are exactly that: statements without evidence. The auditor is accountable for every finding, so each statement, causes included, must be checked against the evidence before issue. A redraft limited to the work papers may reduce invented content, but it is still unchecked output; only the auditor's review makes the findings supportable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because transparency about AI use is good practice. But disclosure explains the method; it does not make an unchecked finding supportable.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because findings are discussed with management. But a cause must come from the auditor's evidence; management's agreement is the auditee's view, not proof.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tighter instructions may curb invented content. But a redraft is still unverified output, and the auditor still owns every statement.

tips: Eliminate: A discloses AI use without verifying anything, and C seeks proof of cause from the auditee instead of the evidence.
Final two: B beats D because a tighter prompt still yields unverified text; only the auditor's check against evidence makes findings supportable.
Exam cue: an AI tool can draft, but the auditor reviews and owns every conclusion. Verify against evidence before disclosure or issue.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Approving an audit AI use
questions.question: An Egyptian cement producer's procurement staff upload supplier invoices and contracts. An audit team's approved generative AI tool will read them to flag possible kickbacks. Which risk should the chief audit executive weigh MOST heavily?

options.A: The tool may flag many innocent invoices as possible kickbacks
options.B: Auditors may need training before writing prompts for the tool
options.C: The vendor may train its models on the documents the tool reads
options.D: Planted text in the documents could make the tool skip items

questions.key_concept: Audit AI tools that read auditee-controlled content can be steered by planted instructions, silently hiding evidence; weigh this before approving the use.
questions.pre_read: Ask who wrote the documents the tool will read and what they would want it to miss.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative tool can treat text it reads as instructions. Here suppliers wrote the files and procurement staff, whose dealings are under review, upload them, so anyone hiding kickbacks could cheaply plant wording that tells the tool to pass over items, and the audit would never see them. False flags are likely too, but they are visible and get followed up; steered misses are silent.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because false flags waste audit effort. But they are visible and followed up; items the tool is steered to skip are never seen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because prompting is a new skill. But training is easily arranged and does not stop the documents themselves steering the tool.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors may reuse inputs. But the tool is approved, so its data terms were already assessed before this use.

tips: Eliminate: C reopens data terms the tool's approval already covered, and B is a training gap that is easily closed.
Final two: D beats A because false flags are visible and followed up, while planted text can silently hide the very items under audit.
Exam cue: when an audit AI tool reads content the auditee controls, weigh indirect prompt injection. The auditee could steer the audit's own tool.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Testing an output filter
questions.question: A Uruguayan children's learning app uses an output filter to stop its tutoring chatbot from showing unsuitable content. Which procedure gives the IS auditor the BEST evidence that the filter operates effectively?

options.A: Inspect the filter's configured block lists and moderation rules
options.B: Count the replies the filter blocked in each month this year
options.C: Send reworded and disguised prompts and inspect the replies
options.D: Read the filter vendor's description of how its filter works

questions.key_concept: AI guardrails are tested by attempting bypasses, such as reworded or disguised prompts; counts of blocked outputs cannot reveal misses.
questions.pre_read: Ask which evidence could show content that got past the filter.
questions.correct_explanation: Filters can often be bypassed by rewording a request or hiding it inside another task, so only trying such prompts shows whether unsuitable content gets through. Run in a test environment agreed with management, the test measures misses directly. Monthly block counts show the filter is active, but they cannot show what it let through, which is the risk to children.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because block lists define the filter. But configuration shows design, not whether reworded prompts can bypass it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because logs show the filter working all year. But blocked replies count catches; content that got through never appears in the count.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors document their products. But a description is the vendor's claim, not evidence of how the filter performs here.

tips: Eliminate: A inspects design rather than operation, and D relies on the vendor's description instead of evidence.
Final two: C beats B because block counts record only catches, while reworded and disguised prompts reveal what gets through.
Exam cue: to test an AI guardrail, try to get past it the way users would. Counts of blocked items never show the misses.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Recommending on a biased model
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that an Austrian bank's voice-authentication model locks out customers with speech impairments far more often than other customers. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner set group lockout limits and fix any breach
options.B: Have the model owner raise the model's overall accuracy target
options.C: Retrain the model on 2,000 hours of speech from affected customers
options.D: Tell customers in the app that voice checks may sometimes fail

questions.key_concept: AI recommendations set group-level outcomes for a named owner; overall accuracy targets can hide a small group's harm, and owners choose the fix.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each proposed measure would reveal the affected group's results, and who designs the fix.
questions.correct_explanation: An overall accuracy figure is dominated by the largest group, so a higher target can be met while customers with speech impairments stay locked out. Lockout limits for each group, owned and acted on by the model owner, make the gap visible and hold someone to closing it. The auditor recommends that outcome and its owner; the owner chooses the technical fix.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because better accuracy sounds like the cure. But an average can rise while a small group's lockouts stay high, so the gap could persist unseen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more representative data often narrows such gaps. But designing the fix is the owner's job; the auditor recommends the result to achieve.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is transparent. But a notice leaves affected customers locked out; it informs without fixing anything.

tips: Eliminate: C has the auditor designing the model fix, and D informs customers without reducing lockouts.
Final two: A beats B because an overall target can be met while one group stays locked out; group limits make the gap visible and owned.
Exam cue: AI recommendations name a measurable outcome for each affected group and an owner. Averages hide small groups, and the fix is the owner's.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Using a validation unit's work
questions.question: A Puerto Rican staffing agency's validation unit is independent of the builders. It reported only overall accuracy for the pay-offer model. IS audit lacks machine-learning skills. How should the IS audit manager BEST use this work?

options.A: Rely on the unit's report, since validators were independent of builders
options.B: Have a co-sourced specialist repeat the unit's accuracy tests
options.C: Use it for accuracy, and co-source tests of offers by worker group
options.D: Ask the builders whether validation covered the pay-offer model's main risks

questions.key_concept: Independent validation can be used for what it tested; the audit fills gaps, such as group fairness, that one accuracy figure cannot show.
questions.pre_read: List what the validation measured, then ask what risk of this model it leaves untested.
questions.correct_explanation: Independent validation can be relied on for what it tested, once the manager has evaluated the unit's competence and method. One overall accuracy figure says nothing about whether pay offers differ unfairly across worker groups, so the manager uses the work for accuracy and fills the gap with a co-sourced specialist. Relying on the report for everything treats independence as coverage; independent work still covers only what it tested.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the validators are independent of the builders. But independence shows objectivity, not coverage; an overall accuracy figure cannot show fair pay offers across groups.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it uses a specialist. But repeating the same accuracy tests duplicates covered work and still leaves pay offers by group untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the builders know the model. But they are the subject of the validation; their view of its coverage is not independent evidence.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats work the unit already covered, and D asks the builders to vouch for a review of their own model.
Final two: C beats A because independence makes the unit's work usable, not complete; overall accuracy cannot show whether pay offers are fair across worker groups.
Exam cue: when using others' AI testing, rely on what it covered and fill the gaps. An overall accuracy figure never answers the fairness question.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Builders' control list
questions.question: A Gambian airline's model overbooks flights that it predicts will have no-shows. The data science team's control list for the model covers validation and drift monitoring. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Scope testing to the listed controls plus IT change controls
options.B: Map the model's risks to controls independently of the list
options.C: Ask the team to confirm in writing that the list is complete
options.D: Check the model card for controls missing from the list

questions.key_concept: The IS auditor maps an AI model's risks to controls independently, rather than testing only the controls its builders describe.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option would add to the audit plan before any testing begins.
questions.correct_explanation: Builders list the controls they run, and an AI model's risks reach beyond them: who can change training data, who approves retraining, whether staff can override an overbooking and how bumped passengers are affected. Mapping risks to controls independently shows which controls should exist before testing begins. Adding IT change controls looks thorough, but a retrain changes the model with no code change.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because change controls look like the missing lifecycle piece. But a retrain changes the model with no code change, and label access and overrides sit outside IT change control.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to close the gap. But a written confirmation from the team is still the team's own view of its controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because model cards describe the model. But the card is the builders' document too, so it shares the list's blind spots.

tips: Eliminate: C turns the team's own view into a signed statement, and D checks a document the same builders wrote.
Final two: B beats A because IT change controls track code, while a retrain changes the model with no code change; an independent risk map finds gaps such as retraining approval.
Exam cue: never let builders' control lists set an AI audit's scope. Map risks to controls yourself, then test.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. AI-written extract query
questions.question: An IS auditor's approved AI assistant wrote the query extracting a Belizean tourism board's tour-guide licensing decisions. The assistant then queried the source system for a total, which matched. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Compare the extract to a total from the system's own reports
options.B: Rely on the match, since the total came from the source system
options.C: Accept the extract, since the assistant is approved for audit use
options.D: Ask the assistant to explain what each of its queries does

questions.key_concept: A reconciliation is independent only if the source total comes from outside the AI tool that wrote the extract query.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced each of the two numbers being compared.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant wrote both queries, so the match checks its work against itself: an AI-written query can drop records through a wrong join, filter or date range, and the same misreading of the schema can shape the total too. A total the assistant did not produce, such as the system's own report, gives an independent check. A source-system figure is independent only when the query behind it is.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the total came from the source system. But the assistant wrote that query too, so one wrong filter or date range can shape both numbers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tool passed the audit function's approval. But approval permits using the tool; it does not show this query returned every record.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to check the logic. But the assistant explaining its own queries can repeat its own mistake.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the tool's approval as proof of this one output, and D asks the tool to check its own work.
Final two: A beats B because a total the same assistant queried is not independent; one misread schema can drop the same records from both counts.
Exam cue: reconcile AI-written extracts to a figure the AI tool did not shape. A total the same assistant queried checks its work against itself.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Scoring an audit tool
questions.question: A Faroese salmon exporter's audit team tuned its AI duplicate-invoice tool on 200 known duplicates, then reported it found 196 of them. What is the GREATEST concern with relying on this result?

options.A: Two hundred known duplicates are too few to tune the tool
options.B: The four missed duplicates were not examined for a common pattern
options.C: The tool vendor's own published accuracy figure was not checked
options.D: The tool was scored on the same cases used to tune it

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool scored on the cases used to tune it overstates performance; validation needs known cases held back from tuning.
questions.pre_read: Read how the result was produced before trusting the number.
questions.correct_explanation: Scoring a tool on the cases used to tune it is like grading an exam the student has already seen: the 98% shows how well it fits those 200, not how many new duplicates it will catch. Validation needs known cases held back from tuning. Studying the four misses could refine the tool, but it still trusts a catch rate that overstates performance.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small tuning sets can limit a tool. But the bigger flaw is scoring it on those same cases, which inflates the result whatever the set's size.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because exceptions deserve follow-up. But the four misses come from the tuning cases; the 98% itself overstates what the tool will catch on new invoices.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors publish figures. But a vendor figure from other data would not validate the tool here either.

tips: Eliminate: C looks to a vendor figure that cannot validate the tool on this data, and A blames the set's size rather than how it was scored.
Final two: D beats B because studying four misses still trusts a catch rate measured on tuning cases; only known cases held back from tuning show what the tool will miss.
Exam cue: validate an audit AI tool on known cases it never saw while being tuned, just as models are tested on held-out data.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. An AI service's web-search feature
questions.question: A Greenlandic municipality's audit team finds that the web-search feature of its approved AI service sends prompt text to a search provider outside the contract. What should the chief audit executive do FIRST?

options.A: Allow its use, since the main service is approved under contract
options.B: Strip names from any prompt that might trigger a web search
options.C: Ask the vendor to confirm the search provider deletes queries
options.D: Disable web search for audit work until its data path is assessed

questions.key_concept: An AI service's approval covers data paths its contract covers; features that send audit data to outside providers need assessment first.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the audit data goes when the feature runs.
questions.correct_explanation: The approval covered the AI service under its contract terms; the search feature sends audit data to a provider those terms do not cover, so the approval does not extend to it. Disabling the feature for audit work keeps data inside the approved boundary while the path is assessed. Stripping names leaves context that can still identify people and does nothing for confidential findings.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the service is approved. But approval rested on contract terms that do not reach the outside search provider.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it reduces personal data. But context can still identify people, and confidential audit facts leave anyway.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seeks assurance. But a vendor's word about a provider outside the contract is not an enforceable term.

tips: Eliminate: A extends an approval past the contract it rested on, and C relies on a vendor's word with no contract behind it.
Final two: D beats B because the feature sends audit data outside the approved boundary; stripping names still lets confidential findings and context leave.
Exam cue: an approved AI service is approved under its terms. A feature that sends data elsewhere is outside the approval until assessed.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Tool rating versus observation
questions.question: Three days' observation shows Isle of Man bank staff bulk-clearing a payment model's flags unread. The audit's AI tool reads only flag statuses and rates the review effective. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The control is ineffective, with a note on why the tool disagrees
options.B: Accept the tool's rating, since it analyzed the whole year's population
options.C: Report both ratings and let management decide which one applies
options.D: Rerun the tool with revised prompts until its rating matches

questions.key_concept: An audit AI tool's rating is an input; when direct evidence contradicts it, the auditor concludes on the evidence and documents why.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tool could see in its data and what only observation could see.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool read only flag statuses, and a flag cleared unread has the same status as one reviewed with care. Observation shows the review does not operate as intended, and the auditor owns the conclusion. Noting why the tool's rating differs keeps the work papers defensible. Full-population coverage cannot outweigh evidence the data never captured.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because full-population analytics sound stronger than three days of observation. But the tool saw only statuses; a flag cleared unread looks the same as one reviewed with care.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems balanced. But the conclusion is the auditor's to reach; management does not choose the audit's ratings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a better prompt may help. But tuning a tool until it agrees is not evidence; observation already shows the failure.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the audit's conclusion to management, and D adjusts the tool until it gives the wanted answer.
Final two: A beats B because the tool judged only flag statuses; an unread clearance has the same status as a careful one, so the auditor's evidence decides.
Exam cue: an audit AI tool's rating is input, never the conclusion. When direct evidence contradicts it, conclude on the evidence and record why they differ.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A specialist's jailbreak tests
questions.question: A Tanzanian mobile bank's assistant app adds a system prompt to a vendor model. All 500 jailbreak attempts by IS audit's independent specialist on the model's API failed. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the vendor to confirm the API model matches the app's model
options.B: Have the specialist rerun the tests through the bank's own app
options.C: Rely on the result, since the bank's app calls the vendor model
options.D: Rely on the result, since the specialist is independent and qualified

questions.key_concept: Judge a specialist's AI test against the system as deployed; bare model API results do not carry over to the app wrapping it.
questions.pre_read: Read the test conditions as closely as the result.
questions.correct_explanation: Using an expert's work means judging whether the method fits the objective. The bank's app adds its own system prompt, and may add data or tools, each of which can change how the model responds, so an attack the bare model refuses can succeed through the app. Rerunning the tests through the app checks the assistant customers use. Sharing one underlying model does not carry API results over.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But a vendor's confirmation is a claim, and the same model can behave differently inside the app.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the model is the same. But the app adds its own prompt and may add data or tools, which can change how attacks land.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the specialist is vetted and independent. But objectivity and skill do not extend tests to a channel never tried.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps a test for the vendor's assurance, and D weighs who ran the tests instead of what they covered.
Final two: B beats C because the app's own system prompt, and any data or tools it adds, can change how the model responds; API results do not carry over to the deployed assistant.
Exam cue: before relying on an AI specialist's result, check that the tests hit the system as deployed: channel, prompts, data, users and version.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. A fairness dashboard's figures
questions.question: A Colombian bank's fairness dashboard compares approval rates by sex using only completed applications. The bank's model asks some applicants for extra documents, and many then withdraw. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the dashboard, since the bank's own systems generate it
options.B: Recompute approval rates by sex from completed applications in the logs
options.C: Recompute approval rates by sex from all applications, withdrawals included
options.D: Ask the model owner why applicants withdraw after document requests

questions.key_concept: When a model's own actions remove people before the decision, fairness is measured on everyone who applied, not only completed cases.
questions.pre_read: Ask who the metric's population leaves out, and why.
questions.correct_explanation: The model does more than approve or decline: its document requests drive withdrawals, so a measure built on completed applications leaves out people the model effectively turned away. If requests fall more on one sex, the dashboard can look fair while the process is not. Recomputing from all applications, withdrawals included, tests the model's whole effect. Reperforming the dashboard's figures only confirms its arithmetic on the same narrowed population.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the figures are system-generated. But the system applies a definition that leaves out applicants the model's requests drove away.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it repeats the dashboard's definition, so withdrawals the model caused stay outside the measure.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seeks the cause. But inquiry comes after evidence; first measure whether withdrawals differ by sex.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a system's figures without checking what they measure, and D asks for explanations before the evidence is in.
Final two: C beats B because reperforming the dashboard repeats its narrowed population; only all applications show whether document requests drove one sex away.
Exam cue: check how a fairness metric's population was formed. If the model's actions remove people early, recompute from everyone who applied.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Preserving a continuously learning model
questions.question: A Bahraini Islamic bank's fraud model updates its weights continuously from each confirmed case. Which preservation request BEST lets the IS auditor later rerun the model on decisions from the audit period?

options.A: The training code and the dataset that built the model's first version
options.B: A full copy of the updated model as it stands at fieldwork
options.C: The decision log of each transaction's score and outcome
options.D: Regular snapshots of the model, with the update data between them

questions.key_concept: A continuously learning model has no fixed version; reperforming past decisions needs periodic snapshots and the update data between them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a later rerun would need to recreate.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that learns from every confirmed case is a slightly different model after each update, so one copy taken at fieldwork reproduces only today's decisions. Regular snapshots, with the confirmed cases applied between them, let the auditor rebuild the model as it stood when a past decision was made, or come close, and rerun it. Decision logs record what was decided, but cannot show the model then in force would decide that way.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it shows how the model began. But thousands of updates have shaped it since; the starting point cannot reproduce later states.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it preserves the model before further change. But it captures only today's state; earlier decisions came from states the updates have replaced.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs are strong evidence of what happened. But they record results; rerunning needs the model state that produced them.

tips: Eliminate: A preserves only the starting point of a model that has changed since, and C records results without the model that produced them.
Final two: D beats B because a continuously learning model changes with each case; one copy at fieldwork cannot rerun decisions made months earlier.
Exam cue: a model that keeps learning has no single version. Preserve regular snapshots and the update data between them to rerun past decisions.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Model-written review reasons
questions.question: A Lebanese retailer's warranty assessors must give reasons for accepting the model's claim rejections. The screen pre-fills model-written reasons, and most keep them. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern with these reasons as evidence?

options.A: They may be too short to explain each rejection fully
options.B: The model-written reasons may contain factual errors about the claims
options.C: They may record the model's text, not any human judgment
options.D: They may not be kept for the whole audit period

questions.key_concept: A pre-filled, model-written reason that reviewers keep evidences the model's text, not human review, and invites automation bias.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each record would look like if no real review took place.
questions.correct_explanation: The reasons field is meant to evidence each assessor's review, but when the screen supplies a model-written reason and most assessors keep it, the field records the model's text, not human judgment. Pre-filled answers also anchor reviewers toward agreement, so the records may reflect automation bias rather than review. The auditor needs other evidence, such as review times, overrides or seeded cases. Errors in the reasons matter, but they do not show whether review happened.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because brief reasons explain little. But length is not the problem; who wrote the reason is.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generated text can be wrong. But the question is whether the field shows review; even accurate text would be the model's, not the assessor's.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retention limits evidence. But nothing suggests a retention gap; the reasons' authorship is the issue.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about length when authorship is at issue, and D raises a retention gap nothing suggests.
Final two: C beats B because even accurate model text, kept unchanged, shows acceptance, not the assessor's judgment.
Exam cue: evidence of human review must come from the human. Pre-filled AI text that reviewers keep signals automation bias, not oversight.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Recommendation on a vendor's silent change
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a Cameroonian bank's vendor-hosted chatbot quoted outdated exchange rates for a month. This began after the vendor changed its data feed without telling the bank. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: The bank's vendor manager should require change notices and retests
options.B: The vendor should restore and retest its exchange-rate data feed
options.C: The bank should pin the chatbot to one fixed model version
options.D: The bank's chatbot team should add a disclaimer that rates may lag

questions.key_concept: Recommendations on vendor AI address the organization's control over every vendor change, with a named internal owner; pinning the model covers only one component.
questions.pre_read: Locate the control gap that let the problem run for a month.
questions.correct_explanation: The finding's cause is the bank's missing control over vendor changes: the vendor changed a feed, and nothing at the bank detected it for a month. The recommendation goes to the bank's management, with an owner who requires notice of vendor changes and retests the chatbot after each one. Pinning the model version sounds like change control, but this change was to a data feed, which a pinned model would still read.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor's change caused the error. But the report recommends to the bank, and fixing one feed leaves the next change undetected.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because version pinning is a sound AI control. But this change came through a data feed; a pinned model still reads whatever the feed supplies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it warns customers. But a disclaimer leaves wrong rates in place and does nothing about changes going unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: B addresses the vendor rather than the bank's control gap, and D warns customers while wrong rates continue.
Final two: A beats C because the change was to a data feed, not the model; only notice and retesting of every vendor change catch it.
Exam cue: an AI system changes through models, data feeds, prompts and settings. Recommend control over every vendor change, not just the model version.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Supervising an AI-assisted work paper
questions.question: A Bangladeshi exporter's IS audit manager finds a work paper. It concludes from an approved AI tool alone that all 650 supplier bank-detail changes had callbacks. Which step BEST supports the conclusion before sign-off?

options.A: Rerun the tool on the same records to confirm its conclusion
options.B: Have the preparer verify a sample against the underlying source records
options.C: Sign off, since the tool is approved for audit testing
options.D: Check the tool's validation record before signing off the work paper

questions.key_concept: Supervising AI-assisted work, the reviewer needs evidence of what the auditor verified; tool approval or validation does not stand in for it.
questions.pre_read: Read the work paper as a reviewer who must sign it.
questions.correct_explanation: Supervision asks whether each conclusion rests on sufficient evidence the auditor checked. Here the work paper holds only the tool's output: nothing shows whether all 650 changes were in its input or whether any callback was confirmed. Having the preparer verify a sample against change and callback records, and document it, gives the conclusion evidence. The tool's validation shows it worked on test cases, not that this run was complete and right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a rerun seems to confirm. But repeating the same tool on the same data checks consistency, not accuracy or completeness.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because approval sounds like assurance. But approval permits use; each conclusion still needs the auditor's own checks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because validation supports reliance. But it shows the tool worked on test cases, not that this run's inputs and results were right.

tips: Eliminate: A checks the tool against itself, and C treats approval of the tool as proof of this result.
Final two: B beats D because validation shows the tool can work, not that this run covered all 650 changes and got them right.
Exam cue: an AI tool's output in a work paper is unfinished work. Supervisors look for the auditor's own checks against source records.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. An advisory model in the plan
questions.question: A Queensland child-safety agency's audit universe rates its hotline-screening model low risk, because caseworkers decide each visit. Caseworkers accept 98% of the model's recommendations, most within seconds. What is the GREATEST weakness in this rating?

options.A: It ignores how advanced the model's machine-learning method is
options.B: It does not show caseworkers are trained and authorized to override
options.C: It credits a caseworker review that rarely changes the outcome
options.D: It should rest on the model's accuracy at launch, not on caseworkers

questions.key_concept: A human step lowers AI risk only if it changes outcomes; fast, near-total agreement means a rating cannot credit the review untested.
questions.pre_read: Compare the rating's reasoning with how decisions are really made.
questions.correct_explanation: A human in the loop lowers risk only if the human changes outcomes. Caseworkers accepting 98% of recommendations within seconds suggests automation bias: the model largely decides which reports get a visit, so its errors become decisions about children's safety. Rating the use low because people decide credits a review that rarely acts. Training and authority to override, even if shown, would not prove the review catches errors.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because complex methods seem riskier. But novelty is not risk; ratings follow the likelihood and impact of harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because trained, authorized reviewers are a real control. But 98% agreement in seconds suggests the review rarely changes outcomes, so paper authority cannot justify a low rating.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because accuracy matters. But launch accuracy says nothing about harm when errors are followed, and the weakness here is crediting a review that rarely acts.

tips: Eliminate: A rates by technical novelty, and D rests the rating on launch accuracy.
Final two: C beats B because override authority on paper does not show the review changes outcomes; 98% agreement in seconds points to automation bias.
Exam cue: when reviewers agree with a model almost always and fast, rate the use as if the model decides, then test the review.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A scam model retrained monthly
questions.question: A Finnish dating service retrains its scam-profile model monthly on moderators' verdicts, and moderators review only the profiles the model flags. Which area is MOST important for the IS auditor to bring into scope?

options.A: Accuracy reported separately for each kind of scam and in total
options.B: How the labels that each retrain learns from are produced
options.C: Backup and recovery of the retraining environment
options.D: Specialist review of the model's neural network architecture

questions.key_concept: A model retrained on outcomes it selected never learns what it misses; scope covers how its labels are produced, not only its accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Follow the model through one monthly cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: Moderators see only what the model flags, so every label it retrains on comes from its own choices. Scam profiles it misses are never reviewed, never labeled and never learned, and the blind spot can widen with each monthly retrain. Scope must cover how labels are produced. Accuracy by scam type is computed from those same self-selected labels, so it would look sound while the blind spot grows.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because overall accuracy can hide weak areas. But every figure uses labels the model chose, so scams it misses never appear in any of them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recovery is a standard control. But it is a minor IT point beside labels that shape every retrain.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the model is complex. But scoping the algorithm leaves out the data, where this risk sits.

tips: Eliminate: D scopes the algorithm rather than its data, and C adds a general IT control of minor weight here.
Final two: B beats A because accuracy by scam type is computed from labels the model itself chose, so the scams it misses never show up.
Exam cue: when a model learns only from cases it selected, scope the labeling loop. What it never flags is never learned or measured.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. A specialist's stand-in model
questions.question: The audit's vetted specialist explains a Kerala cooperative bank's gold-loan model using a simpler surrogate model trained to mimic it, and concludes that declines rest on repayment history. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the conclusion, as the specialist was vetted and is independent
options.B: Compare the surrogate's main factors with the bank's model card
options.C: Check how closely the surrogate's outputs match the real model
options.D: Ask the model's developers to confirm the surrogate's explanation

questions.key_concept: A surrogate model explains itself; its explanations describe the real model only as far as the two agree, so check that agreement first.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the specialist's method can and cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: A surrogate explains itself, not the bank's model. Its factors describe the real model's declines only as far as the two agree, so the first question is fidelity: how often the surrogate reaches the same decision for the same applicants. The model card is written by the builders and describes intended design; agreeing with it cannot show the surrogate tracks what the deployed model actually does.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the specialist was vetted. But vetting covers competence and objectivity, not whether this method supports this conclusion.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the card documents the intended factors. But it is the builders' description, so matching it cannot show the surrogate mirrors the deployed model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because developers know the model. But builders vouching for a test of their own model is weak, non-independent evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a vetted specialist without evaluating the method, and D asks the builders to vouch for a test of their own model.
Final two: C beats B because a surrogate explains the real model only as far as they agree; a builder-written card cannot show that agreement.
Exam cue: an explanation from a stand-in model covers the stand-in. Check how closely it matches the real model before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. An audit tool on the auditee's model
questions.question: A Basque tax agency's AI tool drafted 30,000 taxpayer letters. The agency's IS audit team plans to check them with an approved audit tool built on the same vendor model. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The vendor may update the shared model while the checks run
options.B: The audit tool may share the drafting tool's blind spots
options.C: Checking each of the 30,000 letters costs more than a sample
options.D: The agency's managers have not agreed to the tool's criteria

questions.key_concept: A checker built on the same model as the AI it checks tends to share its blind spots, so it is not an independent test.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern by how much it would weaken the audit's conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: A checker built on the same model as the drafter tends to share its mistakes: if the model misreads a rule, the checker likely accepts the misreading. Its errors are correlated with the drafting tool's, so the letters most likely to be wrong are the ones most likely to pass. A model update during the checks is a reproducibility issue to record; it does not undermine validity the way shared blind spots do.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because hosted models change. Recording the version handles that; shared blind spots would make the checks unreliable even with a fixed version.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because samples are cheaper. But a full-population check is a strength when the tool is valid; cost is not the main risk here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners know their rules. But the auditor selects audit criteria for suitability; management's agreement is never a condition.

tips: Eliminate: C treats full-population testing as the problem, and D gives the auditee a veto over audit criteria.
Final two: B beats A because shared training means shared mistakes; a model update can be recorded, but a checker blind to the same errors passes them.
Exam cue: an AI checking output from the same model is not an independent check. Look for correlated errors before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. A policy rule the tool reported
questions.question: An IS auditor gave an approved AI tool a Guatemalan coffee cooperative's IT policies and nothing else. The tool states that passwords must be at least 12 characters. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Locate the rule in the policy text before relying on it
options.B: Rerun the question to see whether the answer repeats
options.C: Confirm every policy file was supplied to the tool
options.D: Accept it, since these policies were its sole input

questions.key_concept: A generative tool can fill gaps in documents with plausible general knowledge; confirm each statement in the source before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask where a plausible statement like this could have come from.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative tool can blend the documents it was given with what it learned in training, so a common rule such as a 12-character minimum may appear even if the cooperative's policies never say it. The auditor finds the requirement in the policy text before relying on it. Confirming that every policy file was supplied checks the input, but even with every file supplied the tool can add the rule from training.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consistency feels reassuring. But a tool can repeat the same unsupported statement every time.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because missing input often causes wrong answers. But even with every file supplied, the tool can add the rule from training; only the policy text verifies it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool was given nothing else. But generative tools can add plausible rules from training, so the statement may appear in no policy.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a repeated answer as verified, and D accepts the statement because of what the tool was given.
Final two: A beats C because even with every policy file supplied, a generative tool can add a common rule from training; only the policy text shows it exists.
Exam cue: AI statements about documents can come from training rather than the documents. Confirm each one in the source.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. Two prompts, two answers
questions.question: An IS auditor asked an approved AI tool whether 80 firewall rule changes at a Sardinian airport were approved. It said all were. Asked which lacked approval, it named six. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Ask the tool which of its two answers is right
options.B: Treat the six as unapproved, since that prompt was more skeptical
options.C: Check every change against the approval records directly
options.D: Have the tool cite the approval record for each change

questions.key_concept: Generated answers lean toward a question's framing, so two prompts can yield opposite results; neither is evidence until checked against records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the difference between the two answers reveals about both.
questions.correct_explanation: Generated answers tend to follow the framing of the question: asked to confirm, a model leans toward confirming; asked to find faults, it leans toward finding some. Neither answer is evidence. With only 80 changes, the auditor checks each against the approval records. Having the tool cite a record for each change only adds generated text that framing can steer; a cited record proves nothing until opened.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the tool produced both answers. But its verdict on itself is more generated text, not evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a fault-finding question looks like professional skepticism. But framing steers generated answers: some of the six may be invented, and the other 74 stay untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a cited record looks traceable. But a generated citation is more generated text: it can follow the framing or name a record that says otherwise.

tips: Eliminate: A asks the tool to judge itself, and B mistakes a fault-finding prompt for professional skepticism.
Final two: C beats D because a citation the tool writes is more generated text, which framing can steer; only the approval records themselves are evidence.
Exam cue: when rewording a prompt changes the answer, neither answer is evidence. Go to the source records.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. A fake-supplier tool's test result
questions.question: A Dutch flower auction's audit team tested its AI fake-supplier tool on 1,000 supplier records, half of them fake. Precision was 90%. Under 1% of live records are fake. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: A test on 1,000 records says nothing about larger volumes
options.B: The vendor's own accuracy figure should replace this test
options.C: A far larger share of its flags will be false in use
options.D: It may miss kinds of fake suppliers absent from the test set

questions.key_concept: Precision depends on how common the target is; a test set rich in exceptions overstates precision when exceptions are rare in live data.
questions.pre_read: Compare the test conditions with the live data the tool will meet.
questions.correct_explanation: Precision depends on how common the target is. In a test set half full of fake suppliers, false alarms were few beside the many true hits. Live, where fakes are under 1%, the same false-alarm rate applies to almost every record, so most flags may be false and follow-up effort balloons. Missing unseen kinds of fakes is a real risk, but nothing in these facts points to it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because volume grows. But error rates do not depend on volume; the share of fake suppliers is what changed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors publish figures. But a vendor figure is an input, not validation on the auditor's data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because test sets can miss patterns. But the stated fact is the gap between test and live fake rates, which inflates false alarms.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses volume with prevalence, and B swaps validation for a vendor figure.
Final two: C beats D because the facts given are the test and live fake rates; at under 1%, the same tool's flags will be mostly false.
Exam cue: check that an audit tool was validated at a realistic exception rate. Precision measured on balanced data overstates live precision.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Whistleblower notes in an approved service
questions.question: A Sicilian ceramics maker's IS auditor plans to summarize whistleblower notes in an approved AI service. Its contract bars training on inputs but keeps them 30 days for abuse review. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The summary would need disclosing as AI use in the report
options.B: The summary may distort the whistleblower's key allegations
options.C: None, since the contract bars training on the notes
options.D: Provider staff may see who the whistleblower is

questions.key_concept: A bar on training does not bar retention; check an AI service's retention and human-review terms before confidential audit data goes in.
questions.pre_read: Read each contract term for what it does and does not limit.
questions.correct_explanation: A bar on training stops the provider learning from the notes, not keeping them. Here inputs stay 30 days and may be read by provider staff checking for abuse, and allegations are the kind of content such review can flag, so the whistleblower's identity could reach people outside the audit. A distorted summary is a real risk, but the auditor can check it against the notes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because methodology may require disclosure. But disclosure is a reporting step, not the risk of the provider keeping confidential notes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because summaries can be wrong. But the auditor can check a summary against the notes; exposed details cannot be taken back.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a training bar is the protection most often sought. But it does not stop retention or human review of inputs, which this contract allows.

tips: Eliminate: A mistakes a disclosure duty for the main risk, and B names a risk the auditor can check against the notes.
Final two: D beats C because barring training does not bar keeping: inputs held for abuse review can be read by provider staff.
Exam cue: read AI service terms for retention and human review, not just training use, before audit data goes in.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Stating a test result
questions.question: An IS auditor put 200 test questions to a Hungarian vehicle-registration office's assistant in May and found 12 wrong answers. The vendor updates the model monthly. Which condition statement is BEST for the finding?

options.A: Twelve of 200 test answers from May's version were wrong
options.B: Applicants may have missed registration deadlines after wrong answers
options.C: The assistant answers 12 in 200 registration questions wrongly
options.D: May's test accuracy is below an acceptable standard

questions.key_concept: A condition states what was found and on what basis; for a hosted model, tie the result to the version and test that produced it.
questions.pre_read: Check that each statement claims no more than the test showed.
questions.correct_explanation: A condition states what the auditor found, on what basis. Twelve wrong answers came from 200 test questions put to the version live in May; the vendor has updated the model since, and test questions are not a random draw of applicants' questions. Stating a general 6% error rate claims more than the test showed, and management could rightly challenge it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because harm matters. But this is the finding's effect, and stated as possible harm it does not describe what was found.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it uses the test's own figures. But it states them as a general rate for all questions and for versions since May.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it judges performance. But it names no criteria and no result, so it is a conclusion, not a condition.

tips: Eliminate: D gives a judgment with no facts or criteria, and B states the effect rather than the condition.
Final two: A beats C because a monthly-updated model and a set of test questions support a statement about that test and version, not a general rate.
Exam cue: state AI test results with their basis: version, period and sample. Hosted models change, so unqualified rates overclaim.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. A specialist's AI-assisted analysis
questions.question: An external specialist's report for a Bosnian telecom audit says the specialist's network-traffic analysis was AI-assisted. It gives no detail. Before relying on it in the audit report, what should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Find out what the AI did and what the specialist then checked
options.B: Rerun the analysis with the audit team's own approved AI tool
options.C: Reperform a sample of the specialist's reported findings
options.D: Rely on it, since the specialist is responsible for their methods

questions.key_concept: Using another's AI-assisted work, the auditor must learn how the AI was used and what was verified before relying on it as audit evidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the auditor would need to defend this analysis later.
questions.correct_explanation: Using another's work means understanding how it was produced, and part of this work was produced by AI in ways nobody has described. The auditor needs to know what the tool did and which outputs the specialist verified against data before the analysis can support a conclusion the auditor will own. Reperforming a sample of the reported findings checks what the specialist found, not what the AI may have screened out before anyone looked.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems independent. But a different tool's rerun is another unvalidated output, not an understanding of this one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperformance is strong evidence. But it checks only what was reported; it cannot show what the AI screened out before the specialist looked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because specialists own their methods. But the auditor remains responsible for conclusions built on their work.

tips: Eliminate: D shifts accountability to the specialist, and B adds a second unexamined AI output.
Final two: A beats C because reperforming reported findings cannot show what the AI left out; the auditor first learns what it did and what was checked.
Exam cue: AI inside someone else's work is still evidence you own. Learn how it was produced and verified before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: 3A Audit planning and design. Co-sourcing an AI specialist
questions.question: IS audit's co-sourced specialist, who has validated banks' credit-scoring models for years, will assess a Philippine rural bank's AI agent that chats with members and moves funds between their accounts. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Their skills may not cover prompt injection or agent permissions
options.B: IS audit cannot keep responsibility for co-sourced work
options.C: The specialist may have worked for the agent's developer
options.D: Members' chats would be shared outside the bank

questions.key_concept: A specialist must be competent for the AI risks in scope; credit-model validation does not cover prompt injection or agent permissions.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the question actually states.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent that chats with members and moves money is exposed to prompt injection and depends on its tool permissions, risks that years of credit-model validation may never have covered. IS audit must check that the specialist's competence fits these risks before relying on the work. Past ties to the agent's developer would matter, but nothing given suggests any, while the skills gap follows directly from the facts.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because outsiders do the testing. But co-sourcing keeps responsibility with IS audit, which directs and reviews the specialist's work.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because objectivity must always be checked. But nothing suggests ties to the developer here, while the stated skills point to a clear competence gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because chats hold personal data. But specialists work under audit's confidentiality terms; sharing evidence with them is normal.

tips: Eliminate: D treats normal evidence sharing with a bound specialist as the risk, and B misreads co-sourcing, which leaves responsibility with IS audit.
Final two: A beats C because the stated skills do not fit an agent's main risks, while ties to the developer are only a guess here.
Exam cue: Match the specialist to the kind of AI. Statistical modeling skills do not cover agents and language models.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. A withdrawn policy in an answer
questions.question: A Mexican state university's admissions retrieval assistant quoted a fee-waiver policy. The document system shows the policy was withdrawn in March. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor why the assistant could still quote it?

options.A: The vendor's documentation of how its index refreshes
options.B: The document system's record of the March withdrawal
options.C: Staff statements on whether the policy was removed from the index
options.D: The index's log of documents added and removed, with dates

questions.key_concept: A retrieval index is a separate copy of source documents; its own dated records, not the source system's, show what it held.
questions.pre_read: Identify which record each option comes from and what that record can prove.
questions.correct_explanation: A retrieval assistant answers from its own index, a copy built from source documents. Withdrawing the policy in the document system changes the source; the copy changes only if the removal reaches the index. The index's own dated log of additions and removals shows whether the policy was still there when the answer was given, while the withdrawal record shows only that the source changed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it explains the design. But documentation of intended refreshes cannot show what the index held on a given date.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is a system record. But it shows the source changed, not whether the index copy the assistant searched was updated.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because staff manage the index. But statements are weak evidence when a dated system log exists.

tips: Eliminate: C rests on staff statements, and A describes intended refreshes rather than what actually happened.
Final two: D beats B because the assistant searched its own index copy; only the index log shows whether the withdrawal reached it.
Exam cue: For retrieval assistants, evidence comes from the index the model searched, not only the source system.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. A figure from an AI analysis
questions.question: An approved AI tool, writing and running its own code, reports that 7% of an Argentine department-store chain's 60,000 refunds went to staff-held bank accounts. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the tool to explain its matching code step by step
options.B: Review the matching code it ran, then recompute the rate
options.C: Report the 7% as a finding, citing the tool as source
options.D: Trace a sample of the matched refunds to staff payroll records

questions.key_concept: When an AI tool writes and runs its own analysis code, the code is the method; review it and recompute before relying on results.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of the work each option would actually check.
questions.correct_explanation: The 7% rests entirely on code the tool wrote: how it matched account numbers, which refunds it counted and what it divided by. Generated code can join on partial numbers or drop records without any warning. Reviewing that logic and recomputing the rate tests the figure itself. Tracing matched refunds to payroll records confirms single hits, but cannot reveal a wrong match rule, missed matches or a wrong total.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because explanations seem to open the box. But the tool's account of its code is more generated text, not a check of it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the figure looks precise. But unreviewed AI output is a lead; citing the tool does not make the rate right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tracing to source is sound. But it checks only reported matches, not the rule that chose them or the 7% figure.

tips: Eliminate: C reports an unchecked figure, and A asks the tool to vouch for its own work.
Final two: B beats D because tracing hits confirms matches, while the generated code decides what counted as a match and the rate's denominator.
Exam cue: When an AI tool writes its own analysis code, that code is the method. Review it before relying on the numbers.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. An AI tool that found nothing
questions.question: An IS auditor's approved AI search tool finds emails by meaning. It found no emails linking a Ugandan national park authority's procurement officer to a winning supplier. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the tool to list every email it searched
options.B: Rerun the search several times with differently worded questions
options.C: Search the emails for the supplier's names and addresses
options.D: Record that the emails show no dealings with the supplier

questions.key_concept: An AI search finding nothing is not evidence of absence; confirm it with a different method, such as exact searches for names and identifiers.
questions.pre_read: Consider how each option would change the auditor's confidence in the result.
questions.correct_explanation: A search that finds text by meaning ranks emails by similarity; it can miss messages that name the supplier, an account or an invoice number without discussing it in words it matches. Its silence is not evidence of absence. An exact search for the supplier's names and addresses across the email export checks that silence by another method, while rewording still relies on the same tool's sense of meaning.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because coverage matters. But a list the tool writes about itself is more generated output, not proof of what it read.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because framing changes generated results. But every rerun still relies on the same meaning-based ranking that may miss exact names.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool is approved. But a tool's silence is not evidence that no such emails exist.

tips: Eliminate: D treats the tool's silence as proof, and A asks the tool to vouch for its own coverage.
Final two: C beats B because rewording keeps the same meaning-based method; an exact search for names and addresses tests the silence another way.
Exam cue: 'Nothing found' by an AI tool is a result to test, not a conclusion. Check absences with a different method.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Validating a bid-rigging check
questions.question: To spot bid rigging in a Bosnian state electricity company's tenders, an audit team validated a generative AI tool on files from 60 published court cases. The tool caught 58. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The cases may come from other countries' procurement laws
options.B: The tool may have learned these public cases in training
options.C: Sixty published cases are too few to measure a catch rate
options.D: The tool may raise many false alarms on clean tenders

questions.key_concept: Public cases may sit in a generative model's training data, so validating on them can measure memory rather than detection.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the 58 of 60 result would and would not show.
questions.correct_explanation: Published court cases, with their tender files, are public text a generative model may have read in training. If so, catching 58 of 60 can reflect memory of known cases rather than skill at spotting rigging in new tenders, and the rate says little about the company's own files. Sixty cases leave a wide margin of error, but a contaminated set misleads at any size.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because laws differ. But rigging patterns such as rotated bids recur across countries; the larger issue is whether the tool saw these cases.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small samples are imprecise. But 58 of 60 still informs; contamination could make the rate meaningless at any size.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because false alarms cost effort. But false alarms show up when flags are checked, while a catch rate inflated by memory hides missed rigging.

tips: Eliminate: D worries about false alarms that checking flags would expose, and A overstates legal differences when rigging patterns travel.
Final two: B beats C because a larger set of public cases would share the same flaw; the tool may have seen them in training.
Exam cue: Validate generative tools on cases they cannot have seen, such as internal or newly built ones.
