questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. What a work paper records
questions.question: An IS auditor's work paper for an AI-assisted ticket review records the service's 'newest' model alias, temperature 0, every prompt, a hashed input file and three identical runs. What is the GREATEST reproducibility gap?

options.A: Prompts typed in a chat cannot be resubmitted later
options.B: Hosted output can vary between runs, even under one alias
options.C: A hashed input file cannot be opened by a reviewer
options.D: The alias may later point to a newer release

questions.key_concept: A moving model alias points to whatever release the provider makes current, so work papers must record the dated version that actually ran.
questions.pre_read: Check each recorded item against what a reviewer next year would need.
questions.correct_explanation: An alias such as 'newest' is a pointer the provider moves to each new release, so the work paper does not say which model actually ran. A reviewer rerunning it later may get a different model without knowing it, and any difference cannot be explained. Hosted models can vary at temperature 0, but three identical runs suggest that variation was small; the unknown model version is the open gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because chat feels informal. But a recorded prompt can be resubmitted in a chat or a script alike.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because hosted output can vary even at temperature 0. But three identical runs suggest that variation was small; not knowing which model ran is the larger gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because hashes look like encryption. But a hash fingerprints the kept file, proving a reviewer has the same input.

tips: Eliminate: C mistakes a hash for encryption, and A assumes recorded chat prompts cannot be resubmitted.
Final two: D beats B because three identical runs suggest variation was small, while an alias leaves unknown which model a later rerun uses.
Exam cue: Record the exact, dated model version. An alias such as 'newest' can point to a new model without notice.

questions.subtopic: 3E Outputs and reports. Management's response to a chatbot finding
questions.question: A finding says a Portuguese surf school's chatbot invents safety rules, such as allowing beginners to surf alone. In response, management will set the chatbot's temperature to 0. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The setting change may skip change approval and testing
options.B: Customers may find fixed answers repetitive and less helpful
options.C: The vendor may override the setting in an update
options.D: Its answers can stay just as wrong, only more consistent

questions.key_concept: Lowering a model's temperature reduces run-to-run variation, not invented content; an action plan for false answers must reach their cause.
questions.pre_read: Restate the finding before weighing management's plan.
questions.correct_explanation: Temperature controls how much a model's output varies between runs, not whether its statements are true. At 0 the chatbot favors its most likely answer, and a confident invented rule can be exactly that, so beginners may get the same unsafe advice reliably. The setting change should still pass change approval, but even an approved change would leave the finding's cause in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a setting change is a change. But approval governs how a change goes live; an approved setting would still leave the invented rules in place.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because tone affects service. But repetitive wording is a minor cost next to beginners acting on false safety rules.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendors update models. But nothing given suggests an override, and the plan would fail even if the setting held.

tips: Eliminate: B weighs tone above false safety rules, and C rests on a vendor override nothing in the facts suggests.
Final two: D beats A because temperature changes variation, not truth; even a fully approved change leaves the invented rules.
Exam cue: Ask whether management's action reaches the cause. For generative AI, consistent is not the same as correct.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Strata from AI labels
questions.question: An IS auditor plans to stratify a Thai rubber exporter's 9,000 supplier contracts by type for sampling, using labels from an approved AI tool validated at 97% accuracy overall. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Check a sample of the tool's labels against the source files
options.B: Size each stratum by the contract value it holds
options.C: Rely on the labels, given the tool's 97% validated accuracy
options.D: Have procurement staff approve the sample design

questions.key_concept: AI-assigned labels that set strata decide which items can be drawn; check them before relying on the strata they create.
questions.pre_read: Read each option as a step in the sampling plan.
questions.correct_explanation: Stratifying on the tool's labels assumes they are right, and an overall 97% does not show where the other 3% fall. A mislabeled high-risk contract would sit in a stratum where it is unlikely to be drawn, and no later step would reveal it. Checking a sample of labels against the contracts shows whether the strata can be trusted. Sizing strata by value helps only once contracts sit in the right strata.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because value-based sizing is standard. But it weights strata that may hold the wrong contracts if the tool's labels are wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 97% sounds reliable. But errors need not spread evenly; a few in a rare, high-risk type move those contracts into strata unlikely to be drawn.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because procurement knows the contracts. But the auditee approving the audit's sample design would weaken its independence.

tips: Eliminate: B sizes strata before knowing they hold the right contracts, and D gives the auditee a say in the audit's sample design.
Final two: A beats C because an overall 97% does not show where the errors fall; a mislabeled high-risk contract moves out of view, so check labels first.
Exam cue: When AI output shapes a sample, test the output first. A wrong label moves an item out of view.

questions.subtopic: 3B Testing and sampling. Evidence for an escalator failure model
questions.question: A Georgian metro's failure model flags escalator drives. Engineers overhaul every drive it flags and record its condition when opened. Which procedure BEST shows the IS auditor how often the model's flags are right?

options.A: Recompute precision against drive failures recorded over the year
options.B: Compare the wear found inside each flagged drive with its flag
options.C: Rerun each flag's logged sensor inputs through the same model version
options.D: Compare its precision with the drive maker's published failure rates

questions.key_concept: When flags trigger action that prevents the predicted failure, later outcomes cannot fairly score the flags; use evidence the action did not change.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each procedure would compare.
questions.correct_explanation: Every flag triggers an overhaul that removes the wear behind the predicted failure, so flagged drives rarely go on to fail, and failure records would score most correct flags as false alarms. The condition engineers record on opening each flagged drive comes before the overhaul could change it, so it shows whether each flag was right. Recomputing precision against recorded failures, option A, measures outcomes the overhauls prevented.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recomputing a metric gives the auditor direct evidence. But overhauls stop flagged drives failing, so correct flags would count as false alarms.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reperformance shows each flag was raised as logged. But it shows the model ran consistently, not that its flags were right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks give context. But a maker's failure rates describe drives in general, not whether this model's flags were right.

tips: Eliminate: C shows only that each flag was raised as logged, and D compares the model with drives in general.
Final two: B beats A because the overhaul removes the failures A counts; the wear found inside each flagged drive is evidence the action did not change.
Exam cue: When a model's flags trigger action, test the flags on evidence the action could not change.

questions.subtopic: 3C Evidence collection. What a customer was told
questions.question: A Tajik coal merchant's ordering chatbot runs each model reply through an output filter. Which evidence BEST shows the IS auditor what a customer disputing a delivery price was told?

options.A: The model's output log, with version and prompt
options.B: The filter's settings in force on that date
options.C: The customer's own account of the conversation
options.D: The record of each message as displayed

questions.key_concept: When an output filter can rewrite replies, the record of what a person saw is the text as shown, not the model's output.
questions.pre_read: Ask which record would settle the dispute.
questions.correct_explanation: The filter sits between the model and the customer and may rewrite a reply, so the model's output log shows what was generated, not necessarily what appeared on screen. A dispute turns on what the customer was told, which only a record of each message as shown captures. The filter's settings show what it could change, not what it changed in that conversation.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model logs with version and prompt are usually the best record. But the filter may have rewritten the reply after the model wrote it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because settings explain the filter's behavior. But they show what it could change, not what it did to this reply.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the customer was there. But a party's recollection is weaker evidence than a system record of the message as shown.

tips: Eliminate: B shows what the filter could do, not what it did, and C rests on a party's recollection.
Final two: D beats A because a filter that can rewrite replies after the model means the model's log may not be what the customer saw.
Exam cue: Find the last step before the person. When text changes after generation, the evidence is the text as shown.

questions.subtopic: 3D Data quality and analytics. Validating a credit-note screening tool
questions.question: A Sri Lankan apparel maker's audit team validated its AI credit-note screening tool at 95% recall overall. The audit relies on the tool for one rare credit-note type. What does the audit manager MOST need?

options.A: Its precision across the whole validation set
options.B: A rerun of the overall validation on new credit notes
options.C: The vendor's recall for that type at other clients
options.D: Its recall on known credit notes of that type

questions.key_concept: An overall recall can hide poor recall on a rare type; validate an audit tool on the type the audit relies on.
questions.pre_read: Match each figure to the decision the manager must make.
questions.correct_explanation: An overall recall is dominated by common credit-note types, so a rare type can be missed often while the total stays at 95%. The audit relies on the tool for that one type, so its recall must be measured on known credit notes of that type. Precision across the set shows how many flags are false alarms, not how many of the rare credit notes the tool misses.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because false alarms cost effort. But precision measures wrong flags, not the misses the audit's reliance depends on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because new data tests current behavior. But another overall figure can still hide a rare type the tool misses.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it targets the right type. But other clients' credit notes and setup differ; the audit needs its own measured result.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats an overall figure, which blends the rare type into common ones, and C borrows results from other clients' data.
Final two: D beats A because reliance depends on misses of the rare type, which only recall on that type measures; precision counts false alarms.
Exam cue: Validate an audit tool for the job it will do. An overall score can hide the rare case the audit relies on.
